nameStory: The Meadow Slug gets its name from its preference for open, grassy areas and meadow environments where it glides along hunting for tender plant material. Unlike many of its relatives that stick to forests or gardens, this little mollusk has claimed the wide-open spaces as its domain. The 'smooth' part of its genus name Deroceras refers to the sleek, unridged texture of its skin.
description: The Meadow Slug is a small, shell-less mollusk that looks like a tiny, slimy torpedo gliding across the ground. These soft-bodied creatures are typically pale gray to light brown in color and can stretch to about an inch long when fully extended. Like all slugs, they breathe air through a small opening called a pneumostome on their side and leave behind telltale silvery slime trails wherever they go. They're part of the land slug family and spend their lives munching on plants and decomposing organic matter.

idTips.label: Smooth skin texture
idTips.description: The body feels completely smooth to gentle touch, without any ridges, bumps, or rough patches that you might find on other slug species

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and slender, reaching about 1 inch when extended, with a streamlined body that tapers to a point at the tail end

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Pale gray to light brown overall, sometimes with a slightly darker line running down the back, appearing almost translucent in bright light

idTips.label: Breathing hole location
idTips.description: Look for the small, round pneumostome (breathing pore) positioned on the right side of the body, about one-third back from the head

idTips.label: Slime trail
idTips.description: Leaves a thin, silvery mucus trail that dries to a clear, slightly iridescent ribbon - narrower than trails left by larger garden slugs

habitat: Meadow Slugs prefer open, grassy areas like fields, meadows, and lawn edges where the soil stays consistently moist but not waterlogged. They're often found hiding under logs, stones, or leaf litter during the day, emerging at night or after rain to feed. Unlike forest slugs, they seem to thrive in areas with more sun exposure and less dense vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and spring rains provide ideal moist conditions. Look for them emerging from winter hideouts under logs and stones.
seasonality.summer: Active mainly at night or after rain showers when the air is humid. During hot, dry periods they retreat deep into soil cracks or under protective cover.
seasonality.fall: Very active during the cooler, wetter autumn months. This is often the best time to spot them as they feed heavily before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, hiding deep in soil, under logs, or in compost piles. May emerge briefly during warm winter thaws but generally remain dormant.

funFact: Meadow Slugs are hermaphrodites - each individual has both male and female reproductive organs - but they still need to find a partner to mate, and their courtship involves an elaborate dance where they circle each other while leaving intertwining slime trails!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Milky Slug, which is similar in size and habitat, but the Milky Slug has a more distinctly white or cream-colored body and produces more copious amounts of thick, white mucus when disturbed. Memory trick: Meadow Slugs are 'mellow' in color (pale and subdued), while Milky Slugs are notably white.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Meadow Slug' and 'Marsh Slug' interchangeably, this species actually prefers well-drained meadow environments over true marshy wetlands, which can cause confusion when trying to predict where to find them based on name alone.
compareHints: Compared to its close relatives, the Meadow Slug is distinguished by its completely smooth skin and preference for open habitats. The Milky Slug has similar smooth skin but produces much more white mucus and tends to be paler, while the Chestnut Slug has a darker, more brownish coloration and slightly rougher skin texture. All three are small compared to the large garden slugs most people know.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The milky slug is smaller than the meadow slug and produces much more noticeable white mucus when disturbed.

Compared to its relatives in New England, the Chestnut Slug is distinguished by its warm brown coloration - the Milky Slug tends to be grayer and produces more obvious white mucus, while the Meadow Slug is typically smaller and paler.
